title: Habakkuk 3:1–15
context: Chapter 3 is a psalm, introduced as “A prayer of Habakkuk, the prophet, set to victorious music” (3:1). The Hebrew term behind “set to victorious music” is uncertain in meaning; it is usually treated as a musical or literary notation. The word “Selah” appears in verses 3, 9, and 13, as it does in many psalms; it is a notation whose meaning is uncertain, perhaps marking a musical or liturgical pause. After a short petition, “In wrath, you remember mercy” (3:2), the psalm describes God coming in power: from Teman and Mount Paran, regions to the south often associated with Edom and the Sinai wilderness, though their exact locations are uncertain (3:3; compare Deuteronomy 33:2; Judges 5:4). The theophany draws on memories of the exodus, the sea, Sinai, and the conquest, including the sun and moon standing still (3:11; compare Joshua 10:12–13), and ends with God trampling the sea (3:15). These verses form one unit and are read together here. In verse 13, “your anointed” may refer to the king, the people, or a future anointed one, and readers in both traditions hold differing views. Shared ground: both traditions read the psalm as remembering God’s past deliverance in order to trust him for the future, and both hear the petition for mercy in wrath as the heart of the prayer.

verses.text: A prayer of Habakkuk, the prophet, set to victorious music.
verses.arminianNotes: “A prayer of Habakkuk, the prophet, set to victorious music.” The heading marks a change from dialogue to psalm. Arminian readers see the prophet who complained now praying, a model of faith that moves from questions to worship without denying the questions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the heading as presenting the chapter as a liturgical prayer, perhaps meant for public use, given the musical notation at its close (3:19). Shared ground: both traditions note that the Hebrew term behind “set to victorious music” is uncertain, often treated as a musical or literary notation, and both read the prayer as the fitting response to the LORD’s answer.

verses.text: LORD, I have heard of your fame. I stand in awe of your deeds, LORD. Renew your work in the middle of the years. In the middle of the years make it known. In wrath, you remember mercy.
verses.arminianNotes: “LORD, I have heard of your fame. I stand in awe of your deeds, LORD.” Habakkuk asks God to “Renew your work in the middle of the years.” Arminian readers hear a genuine petition and treasure “In wrath, you remember mercy” as the plea of one who knows judgment is coming yet appeals to God’s compassion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prayer resting on God’s past deeds and covenant character, trusting that mercy in wrath flows from his own faithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions hear “In wrath, you remember mercy” as central to the prayer and see awe as the right posture.

verses.text: God came from Teman, the Holy One from Mount Paran. Selah. His glory covered the heavens, and his praise filled the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: “God came from Teman, the Holy One from Mount Paran. Selah.” Teman and Paran lie to the south, associated with Edom and the wilderness near Sinai, though their exact locations are uncertain. Arminian readers see the LORD coming as he did of old to save his people, recalled to strengthen faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the theophany echoing older poems of God’s march from the south (compare Deuteronomy 33:2; Judges 5:4), presenting the God of Sinai as the one who will act again. Shared ground: both traditions read the geography as evoking the exodus and Sinai, treat “Selah” as a notation of uncertain meaning, and see his glory filling heaven and earth.

verses.text: His splendor is like the sunrise. Rays shine from his hand, where his power is hidden.
verses.arminianNotes: “His splendor is like the sunrise. Rays shine from his hand, where his power is hidden.” Arminian readers see God’s glory revealed yet still veiled, inviting awe and trust in a power that exceeds what is seen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that even in a blaze of revelation, God’s power remains “hidden,” beyond full human comprehension. Shared ground: both traditions read the light imagery as theophany language, acknowledge that the details of the image are difficult, and see God’s revealed glory as only a glimpse of his greater majesty.

verses.text: Plague went before him, and pestilence followed his feet.
verses.arminianNotes: “Plague went before him, and pestilence followed his feet.” Arminian readers see judgment attending God’s coming, recalling the plagues on Egypt, as he moves to deliver his people and judge their oppressors.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see plague and pestilence as servants in God’s train, under his command, emphasizing his sovereignty over every force of judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetic imagery recalling the exodus, and some readers note ancient Near Eastern parallels in which such figures attend a deity, a comparison held with caution.

verses.text: He stood, and shook the earth. He looked, and made the nations tremble. The ancient mountains were crumbled. The age-old hills collapsed. His ways are eternal.
verses.arminianNotes: “He stood, and shook the earth. He looked, and made the nations tremble.” Arminian readers see creation and the nations responding to God’s presence, a reminder that his ways are eternal while the ancient mountains crumble.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress “His ways are eternal” as the theological center of the verse: what seems permanent collapses before the everlasting God. Shared ground: both traditions read the shaking of earth and nations as theophany imagery, perhaps recalling Sinai (compare Exodus 19:18), and both find in God’s eternal ways a ground for confidence.

verses.text: I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction. The dwellings of the land of Midian trembled.
verses.arminianNotes: “I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction. The dwellings of the land of Midian trembled.” Arminian readers see peoples of the southern wilderness trembling at God’s approach, recalling his past victories on Israel’s behalf.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the fear of these peoples as the fitting response to God’s sovereign march. Shared ground: both traditions note that Cushan is uncertain, often taken as a people near Midian, and that some connect it with the Cushite wife of Moses (Numbers 12:1), though this is debated; both read the verse as recalling the wilderness era.

verses.text: Was the LORD displeased with the rivers? Was your anger against the rivers, or your wrath against the sea, that you rode on your horses, on your chariots of salvation?
verses.arminianNotes: “Was the LORD displeased with the rivers?” The question recalls the sea and the Jordan (compare Exodus 14; Joshua 3). Arminian readers see that God’s battle is not really against water but on behalf of his people, as the “chariots of salvation” show.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD as divine warrior commanding creation, and note that his wrath against the sea serves the salvation of his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the rhetorical question as pointing to the exodus and Jordan crossings, note that some see an echo of ancient imagery of a deity subduing the sea, and see the purpose as salvation.

verses.text: You uncovered your bow. You called for your sworn arrows. Selah. You split the earth with rivers.
verses.arminianNotes: “You uncovered your bow. You called for your sworn arrows. Selah.” Arminian readers see the divine warrior acting faithfully to his sworn promises, the arrows of judgment loosed for his people’s sake.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress “sworn arrows” as acts bound to God’s oath, so that his judgments carry out what he has pledged. Shared ground: both traditions acknowledge that the Hebrew of this verse is difficult, treat “Selah” as a notation of uncertain meaning, and read “You split the earth with rivers” as creation responding to God’s power.

verses.text: The mountains saw you, and were afraid. The storm of waters passed by. The deep roared and lifted up its hands on high.
verses.arminianNotes: “The mountains saw you, and were afraid.” Arminian readers see the whole created order reacting to God’s coming, a picture that makes human resistance seem futile and humble trust the only fitting response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the deep that “lifted up its hands on high” as creation’s submission to its Creator. Shared ground: both traditions read the personification of mountains and deep as theophany poetry, compare Psalm 77:16–19, where the waters see God and are afraid, and see the verse as continuing the exodus imagery of the psalm.

verses.text: The sun and moon stood still in the sky at the light of your arrows as they went, at the shining of your glittering spear.
verses.arminianNotes: “The sun and moon stood still in the sky.” Arminian readers hear an echo of Joshua 10:12–13, where God fought for Israel, and they see the past deliverance recalled to strengthen present faith in the same God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the heavenly bodies halted “at the light of your arrows” as God’s command over creation in the service of his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetic recollection, likely of Joshua 10, without needing to settle how that event occurred, and both see the arrows and spear as images of divine victory.

verses.text: You marched through the land in wrath. You threshed the nations in anger.
verses.arminianNotes: “You marched through the land in wrath. You threshed the nations in anger.” Arminian readers see judgment on the nations as God’s response to their wickedness and their oppression of his people, not as arbitrary anger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign wrath against the nations as the backdrop of salvation, and read “threshed” as an image of decisive judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as recalling the conquest era, note that the wrath serves the purpose stated in verse 13, and refuse to treat the imagery as license for human violence.

verses.text: You went out for the salvation of your people, for the salvation of your anointed. You crushed the head of the land of wickedness. You stripped them head to foot. Selah.
verses.arminianNotes: “You went out for the salvation of your people, for the salvation of your anointed.” Arminian readers see the purpose of the theophany: salvation, achieved as God crushes “the head of the land of wickedness.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress God’s covenant faithfulness to his people and his anointed, and many hear messianic overtones in “your anointed.” Shared ground: both traditions note that “anointed” may refer to the king, to the people, or to a future anointed one, readings found in both traditions, and both treat “Selah” as a notation of uncertain meaning.

verses.text: You pierced the heads of his warriors with their own spears. They came as a whirlwind to scatter me, gloating as if to devour the wretched in secret.
verses.arminianNotes: “You pierced the heads of his warriors with their own spears.” Arminian readers see the oppressor’s weapons turned against him, a fitting reversal for those who came “to scatter me, gloating as if to devour the wretched in secret.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same reversal as God’s justice protecting “the wretched” from those who prey on them. Shared ground: both traditions acknowledge that the Hebrew is difficult, read the verse as divine victory over the enemy, and note that the prophet speaks of the attack as aimed at himself, identifying with his people.

verses.text: You trampled the sea with your horses, churning mighty waters.
verses.arminianNotes: “You trampled the sea with your horses, churning mighty waters.” Arminian readers see the theophany closing with the sea, recalling God’s deliverance at the Red Sea as the pattern for future rescue of his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the final image of God trampling the sea as sovereign mastery over chaos and enemy alike. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as completing the exodus imagery of the psalm, and both see the remembered victory as the ground for the trust and joy expressed in verses 16–19.
